reminder: A transfinite composite is the canonical map from the start of an ordinal-indexed chain to its colimit.
definition: Let $\lambda$ be an [ordinal](c:ordinal) and let $X_0\to X_1\to\cdots$ be a chain of morphisms in a [category](c:category) $C$, indexed by the ordinals $\alpha<\lambda$, such that $X_\beta=\operatorname{colim}_{\alpha<\beta}X_\alpha$ for every limit ordinal $\beta<\lambda$. The transfinite composite of the chain is the canonical morphism $X_0\to\operatorname{colim}_{\alpha<\lambda}X_\alpha$ into the [colimit](c:colimit) of the chain.
examples: For $\lambda=\omega$, a sequence $X_0\to X_1\to X_2\to\cdots$ has the transfinite composite $X_0\to\operatorname{colim}_nX_n$.
In sets, a chain of inclusions $A_0\subseteq A_1\subseteq\cdots$ has the transfinite composite $A_0\hookrightarrow\bigcup_nA_n$.
The small object argument builds a transfinite composite of pushouts of the generating maps.
Non-example: a chain with $X_\omega$ strictly larger than $\operatorname{colim}_nX_n$ is not continuous at the limit ordinal $\omega$, so it is not a chain of this kind.

steps: Regard the ordinal $\lambda$ as a [partial order](c:partial-order), and so as a category with one morphism $\alpha\to\beta$ when $\alpha\le\beta$.
A chain $X:\lambda\to C$ is then a diagram in $C$.
Its transfinite composite is the leg $X_0\to\operatorname{colim}X$ of the colimit cocone.
So a transfinite composition is a colimit of a well-ordered chain, with the extra condition that the chain is continuous at limit ordinals.
links.why: It shows that a transfinite composite is a colimit leg, so results about colimits apply to it.

reminder: A set is transitive when every element of an element of it is also an element of it.
definition: A [set](c:set) $S$ is transitive when $a\in b\in S$ implies $a\in S$. Equivalently, every [element](c:element) of $S$ is a [subset](c:subset) of $S$. This does not say that the [membership relation](c:membership-relation) is a transitive relation on $S$.
examples: The sets $\varnothing$, $\{\varnothing\}$ and $\{\varnothing,\{\varnothing\}\}$ are transitive.
Every von Neumann ordinal is a transitive set.
Non-example: $\{\{\varnothing\}\}$ is not transitive, because $\varnothing\in\{\varnothing\}\in\{\{\varnothing\}\}$ but $\varnothing\notin\{\{\varnothing\}\}$.

steps: Let $\alpha$ be a von Neumann ordinal, so $\alpha$ is the set of all smaller ordinals.
If $a\in b\in\alpha$, then $b<\alpha$ and $a<b$, so $a<\alpha$ and $a\in\alpha$.
Hence $\alpha$ is a transitive set.
An [ordinal](c:ordinal) adds the condition that $\in$ is a well-order on the set.
links.why: It shows that an ordinal is a transitive set with one more condition, a well-ordering by membership.

reminder: A translation moves every point of a space by the same fixed vector.
definition: Let $V$ be an [abelian group](c:abelian-group), for example a [vector space](c:vector-space). The translation by $a\in V$ is the map $T_a:V\to V$ with $T_a(x)=x+a$. It acts on a [function](c:function) $f$ on $V$ by $(\tau_af)(x)=f(x-a)$, which moves the graph of $f$ by $a$.
examples: On $\mathbb{R}$, the map $T_3(x)=x+3$ shifts the line by $3$.
The translate of the bump $e^{-x^2}$ by $a$ is the bump $e^{-(x-a)^2}$ centred at $a$.
Translations compose by $T_aT_b=T_{a+b}$, so they form a group.
Non-example: the maps $x\mapsto2x$ and $x\mapsto-x$ are not translations, because they fix $0$, while a translation by $a\neq0$ fixes no point.

steps: Take $V=\mathbb{R}^n$ with the Euclidean distance $d(x,y)=|x-y|$.
Then the distance between $T_ax$ and $T_ay$ is $|(x+a)-(y+a)|=|x-y|$.
So $T_a$ preserves distance and is an [isometry](c:isometry).
The translation adds the condition that every point moves by the same vector.
links.why: It shows that every fact about isometries also holds for translations.

reminder: A transposition is a permutation that swaps two elements and fixes all other elements.
definition: A transposition of a set $X$ is a [permutation](c:permutation) $(a\ b)$ that exchanges two distinct elements $a$ and $b$ and fixes every other element of $X$. It is a cycle of length $2$.
examples: In the [symmetric group](c:symmetric-group) $S_3$, the transpositions are $(1\ 2)$, $(1\ 3)$ and $(2\ 3)$.
Every transposition is its own inverse, because $(a\ b)(a\ b)$ is the identity.
Every permutation of a finite set is a product of transpositions.
Non-example: $(1\ 2)(3\ 4)$ is not a transposition, because it moves four elements.

steps: A cycle of length $k$ sends $a_1\mapsto a_2\mapsto\cdots\mapsto a_k\mapsto a_1$ and fixes every other element.
Take the case $k=2$ in this definition.
Then $a_1\mapsto a_2\mapsto a_1$, so the cycle swaps $a_1$ and $a_2$.
Hence a transposition is a [cycle](c:cycle-of-a-permutation) of length $2$.
links.why: It shows that transpositions are the shortest cycles that a permutation can have.

reminder: A transvection fixes a hyperplane pointwise and shifts every vector by a multiple of one fixed vector in that hyperplane.
definition: A transvection of a [vector space](c:vector-space) $V$ is a [linear map](c:linear-map) $T(x)=x+\varphi(x)v$, where $\varphi$ is a nonzero linear functional and $v\neq0$ is a vector with $\varphi(v)=0$. It fixes the [hyperplane](c:hyperplane) $\ker\varphi$ pointwise, and it moves every other vector in the direction of $v$. This is the linear-algebra sense of the word.
examples: In the plane, the matrix $\begin{pmatrix}1&t\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ with $t\neq0$ is a transvection with $v=e_1$ and $\varphi(x)=tx_2$.
Each [elementary matrix](c:elementary-matrix) $I+tE_{ij}$ with $i\neq j$ and $t\neq0$ is a transvection.
Every transvection has determinant $1$, so it lies in the [special linear group](c:special-linear-group).
Non-example: the map $\operatorname{diag}(1,2)$ is not a transvection, because it has determinant $2$ and scales $e_2$ instead of shifting along a fixed direction.

reminder: A trapped surface is a closed spacelike surface from which both families of future light rays converge.
definition: A trapped surface in a time-oriented [Lorentzian manifold](c:lorentzian-manifold) (a [spacetime](c:spacetime)) is a compact spacelike $2$-surface $S$ such that both future-directed [null congruences](c:null-congruence) orthogonal to $S$ have negative expansion at every point of $S$. That is, $\theta_+<0$ and $\theta_-<0$, so the cross-section area of each bundle of light rays shrinks at first order.
examples: In Schwarzschild spacetime of mass $M$, every round sphere of constant radius $r<2M$ and constant time inside the black hole is trapped.
A star that collapses past a critical density forms trapped surfaces; this is the starting point of Penrose's singularity theorem.
Non-example: a round sphere in Minkowski space is not trapped, because its outgoing light rays spread apart and $\theta_+>0$.

reminder: A trigonometric function is built from sine and cosine, the coordinates of a point that moves on the unit circle.
definition: On the unit [circle](c:circle), the point reached after arc length $t$ from $(1,0)$ has the coordinates $(\cos t,\sin t)$, which define the functions $\cos$ and $\sin$ on the [real numbers](c:real-number). A trigonometric function is one of $\sin$, $\cos$, $\tan=\sin/\cos$, $\cot$, $\sec$, $\csc$, or a function built from these by sums, products and quotients.
examples: The functions $\sin t$ and $\cos t$ satisfy $\cos^2t+\sin^2t=1$.
The function $\tan t=\sin t/\cos t$ is trigonometric, and it is defined where $\cos t\neq0$.
The function $\sin(2t)=2\sin t\cos t$ is trigonometric, and so is $\cos t+\sin t$.
Non-example: the function $e^t$ is not trigonometric, because it is not built from $\sin$ and $\cos$ by sums, products and quotients.

steps: Take the point $(\cos t,\sin t)$ on the unit circle at arc length $t$.
Its second coordinate is $\sin t$, so [sine](c:sine) is one of the basic trigonometric functions.
It is the special case where the function is a coordinate itself, not a ratio or a product.
links.why: It shows that sine is the coordinate function from which the whole family is built.

steps: Adding $2\pi$ to $t$ returns to the same point $(\cos t,\sin t)$ on the unit circle.
So $\sin(t+2\pi)=\sin t$ and $\cos(t+2\pi)=\cos t$.
A sum, product or quotient of functions with period $2\pi$ also has period $2\pi$.
Hence every trigonometric function is a [periodic function](c:periodic-function), with period $2\pi$ or a divisor of it.
links.why: It shows that every trigonometric function repeats, so one period of the circle gives all values.

reminder: The Turán graph $T(n,r)$ is the complete $r$-partite graph on $n$ vertices whose parts have nearly equal sizes.
definition: Let $n\ge r\ge1$. The Turán graph $T(n,r)$ is the [graph](c:graph) on $n$ [vertices](c:vertex) whose vertex set splits into $r$ parts with sizes that differ by at most $1$, and in which two vertices are joined by an [edge](c:edge) exactly when they lie in different parts.
examples: The graph $T(6,3)$ is the complete tripartite graph $K_{2,2,2}$, the graph of the octahedron.
The graph $T(n,2)$ is the complete bipartite graph $K_{\lfloor n/2\rfloor,\lceil n/2\rceil}$.
Non-example: the star $K_{1,3}$ is complete bipartite on $4$ vertices, but its parts have sizes $1$ and $3$, so it is not $T(4,2)=K_{2,2}$.

steps: Take $r=n$ in the Turán graph $T(n,r)$.
The $n$ parts have sizes that differ by at most $1$ and add up to $n$, so each part has one vertex.
Any two vertices lie in different parts, so every pair is joined by an edge.
Hence $T(n,n)$ is the [complete graph](c:complete-graph) $K_n$.
links.why: It shows that the complete graph is the Turán graph with the most parts.

reminder: The Turing jump of a set $A$ is the halting set of the oracle machines that use $A$ as oracle.
definition: For a set $A\subseteq\mathbb{N}$ of [natural numbers](c:natural-number), the Turing jump $A'$ is the set of all $e$ such that the [oracle machine](c:oracle-machine) with index $e$, run with oracle $A$ on input $e$, halts. It is the [halting problem](c:halting-problem) relative to $A$.
examples: The jump $\varnothing'$ of the empty set is the ordinary halting set.
The jump $\varnothing''=(\varnothing')'$ is strictly harder than the halting set.
For every $A$, the set $A$ is computable from $A'$, but $A'$ is not computable from $A$.
Non-example: no set $A$ equals its own jump $A'$, because $A'$ is never computable from $A$.

steps: Take the empty oracle $A=\varnothing$.
An oracle machine with an empty oracle is an ordinary [Turing machine](c:turing-machine).
So $\varnothing'$ is the set of $e$ such that machine $e$ halts on input $e$.
This set is the [halting problem](c:halting-problem), so the Turing jump relativizes it to any oracle.
links.why: It shows that the jump repeats the halting problem at every level of difficulty.

reminder: A unit of a ring is an element with a two-sided multiplicative inverse, and the unit element $1$ is one of them.
definition: In a [ring](c:ring) $R$, the unit element is the neutral element $1$ with $1a=a1=a$ for all $a\in R$. An element $u\in R$ is a unit when some $v\in R$ has $uv=vu=1$, that is, when $u$ is an [invertible element](c:invertible); the unit element is a unit.
examples: In $\mathbb{Z}$, the units are $1$ and $-1$.
In a [field](c:field), every nonzero element is a unit.
In the matrix ring $M_n(\mathbb{R})$, the units are the invertible matrices.
Non-example: $2$ is not a unit of $\mathbb{Z}$, because $2v=1$ has no integer solution, and $0$ is not a unit unless the ring is zero.

steps: View the multiplication of $R$ as a [monoid](c:monoid) with neutral element $1$.
An invertible element of this monoid is an element $u$ with $uv=vu=1$ for some $v$.
That is exactly the condition for $u$ to be a unit of $R$.
So a unit of a ring is an invertible element of its multiplicative monoid.
links.why: It shows that units of a ring are the invertible elements of one monoid, so monoid results apply.

reminder: Unitarity means that an operator $U$ satisfies $U^\dagger U=UU^\dagger=1$, so it preserves inner products and total probability.
definition: A linear [operator](c:operator) $U$ on a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) is unitary when $U^\dagger U=UU^\dagger=1$, where $U^\dagger$ is the [adjoint operator](c:adjoint-operator). Then $\langle U\psi,U\phi\rangle=\langle\psi,\phi\rangle$ for all vectors, so $U$ keeps lengths and total probability. In physics, unitarity of a scattering matrix $S$ is the condition $S^\dagger S=1$.
examples: A rotation of the plane and the phase factor $e^{i\theta}$ are unitary.
The time evolution $e^{-itH/\hbar}$ of a [self-adjoint](c:self-adjoint-operator) operator $H$ is unitary, so total probability stays $1$.
The Fourier transform is a unitary operator on $L^2(\mathbb{R})$.
Non-example: scaling by $2$ is not unitary, because $U^\dagger U=4\neq1$, and a projection onto a line is not unitary, because it is not invertible.

steps: Take a real matrix $Q$ with $Q^TQ=QQ^T=1$.
For a real matrix, the conjugate transpose $Q^\dagger$ equals the transpose $Q^T$.
So $Q^\dagger Q=QQ^\dagger=1$, and $Q$ is unitary.
Hence the [orthogonal group](c:orthogonal-group) is the part of the unitary matrices that has real entries.
links.why: It shows that unitarity is the complex version of orthogonality.

steps: For a unitary $U$, the norm satisfies $\|U\psi\|^2=\langle\psi,U^\dagger U\psi\rangle=\|\psi\|^2$.
So $\|U\psi-U\phi\|=\|\psi-\phi\|$, and $U$ preserves distances.
The relation $UU^\dagger=1$ gives the inverse $U^\dagger$, so $U$ is onto.
Hence a unitary operator is a linear and bijective [isometry](c:isometry).
links.why: It shows that a unitary operator is exactly a linear isometry of a Hilbert space onto itself.

reminder: Two matrices $A$ and $B$ are unitarily equivalent when $B=U^\dagger AU$ for some unitary matrix $U$.
definition: Matrices $A,B\in M_n(\mathbb{C})$ are unitarily equivalent when $B=U^\dagger AU$ for some [unitary](c:unitary-operator) matrix $U$. For operators $A$ on $H$ and $B$ on $K$, it means $B=WAW^{-1}$ for some unitary map $W:H\to K$ between [Hilbert spaces](c:hilbert-space).
examples: Every normal matrix is unitarily equivalent to the diagonal matrix of its eigenvalues.
The matrices $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$ are unitarily equivalent.

Non-example: $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&2\end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&2\end{pmatrix}$ have the same eigenvalues, but they are not unitarily equivalent, because the second is normal and the first is not.

reminder: The unitization of a C*-algebra $A$ is a unital C*-algebra that contains $A$ as an ideal of codimension one.
definition: The unitization of a [C*-algebra](c:c-star-algebra) $A$ is the vector space $A\oplus\mathbb{C}$ (a [direct sum](c:direct-sum)) with the product $(a,\lambda)(b,\mu)=(ab+\lambda b+\mu a,\lambda\mu)$, the [involution](c:involution) $(a,\lambda)^*=(a^*,\bar\lambda)$ and a norm that makes it a C*-algebra. The new unit is $(0,1)$, and $A$ is the ideal of the elements $(a,0)$.
examples: For $A=C_0(X)$ with $X$ locally compact Hausdorff and not compact, the unitization is $C(X^+)$, the continuous functions on the [one-point compactification](c:one-point-compactification).
The algebra $C_0(\mathbb{R})$ has the unitization $C(S^1)$.
For the compact operators $K(H)$ on an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space, the unitization is $K(H)+\mathbb{C}1$ inside $B(H)$.
Non-example: the direct sum $A\oplus\mathbb{C}$ with the componentwise product is not the unitization, because it has no unit when $A$ has none.

steps: Let $X$ be a locally compact Hausdorff space and let $A=C_0(X)$, a commutative C*-algebra.
A function on $X^+=X\cup\{\infty\}$ is continuous exactly when its restriction to $X$ is continuous and tends to a limit $\lambda$ at $\infty$.
Such a function has the form $f+\lambda1$ with $f\in C_0(X)$, so $C(X^+)=A\oplus\mathbb{C}1$ is the unitization of $A$.
So the unitization extends the [one-point compactification](c:one-point-compactification) from spaces to non-commutative spaces.
links.why: It shows that the unitization is the algebraic form of the one-point compactification.

reminder: The upper half plane is the set of complex numbers whose imaginary part is positive.
definition: The upper half plane is $\mathbb{H}=\{z\in\mathbb{C}\mid\operatorname{Im}z>0\}$, the set of [complex numbers](c:complex-number) above the real axis. It is an open subset of the plane and it does not contain the real axis.
examples: The numbers $i$, $1+2i$ and $-3+\tfrac12i$ lie in $\mathbb{H}$.
The group $SL_2(\mathbb{R})$ acts on $\mathbb{H}$ by $z\mapsto(az+b)/(cz+d)$, and modular forms are functions on $\mathbb{H}$.
Non-example: the number $2$ is not in $\mathbb{H}$, because $\operatorname{Im}2=0$, and $-i$ is not in $\mathbb{H}$, because its imaginary part is negative.

steps: A half-plane is one of the two open regions into which a line cuts the plane.
Take the real axis as the line.
The region above it is $\{z\mid\operatorname{Im}z>0\}$.
So $\mathbb{H}$ is the half-plane that the real axis bounds and that contains $i$.
links.why: It shows that the upper half plane is one particular half-plane of the complex plane.

reminder: A $v_n$ self-map is a map $\Sigma^dX\to X$ that is an isomorphism in $K(n)$-theory and nilpotent in every other $K(m)$.
definition: Fix a prime $p$ and let $X$ be a [finite spectrum](c:finite-spectrum) of type $n$, so that $K(m)_*X=0$ for $m<n$ and $K(n)_*X\neq0$, where $K(m)$ is [Morava K-theory](c:morava-k-theory). A $v_n$ self-map of $X$ is a map $f:\Sigma^dX\to X$ with $d>0$ from a [suspension](c:suspension) of $X$ such that $K(n)_*f$ is an isomorphism and $K(m)_*f$ is nilpotent for every $m\neq n$.
examples: For odd $p$, Adams' map $\Sigma^{2p-2}M(p)\to M(p)$ on the mod $p$ Moore spectrum is a $v_1$ self-map.
The periodicity theorem of Hopkins and Smith says that every finite spectrum of type $n$ has a $v_n$ self-map.
Non-example: the identity map of a type $n$ spectrum $X$ is not a $v_n$ self-map, because it has degree $0$ and is not nilpotent on $K(m)_*X\neq0$ for $m>n$.

reminder: A valuation ring is an integral domain $O$ in which, for every nonzero $x$ of its fraction field, $x$ or $x^{-1}$ lies in $O$.
definition: An [integral domain](c:integral-domain) $O$ with [field of fractions](c:field-of-fractions) $K$ is a valuation ring when, for every nonzero $x\in K$, at least one of $x$ and $x^{-1}$ lies in $O$. Equivalently, the ideals of $O$ are totally ordered by inclusion.
examples: Every [field](c:field) is a valuation ring of itself.
The localization $\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$ of $\mathbb{Z}$ at a prime $p$ is a valuation ring in $\mathbb{Q}$.
The ring $k[[t]]$ of formal power series is a valuation ring in the field $k((t))$.
Non-example: $\mathbb{Z}$ is not a valuation ring in $\mathbb{Q}$, because neither $2/3$ nor $3/2$ is an integer.

steps: Let $O$ be a [discrete valuation ring](c:discrete-valuation-ring) with fraction field $K$ and valuation $v:K^\times\to\mathbb{Z}$.
Then $O$ consists of $0$ and the elements $x$ with $v(x)\ge0$.
For nonzero $x\in K$, either $v(x)\ge0$, or $v(x^{-1})=-v(x)>0$.
So $x$ or $x^{-1}$ lies in $O$, and $O$ is a valuation ring with value group $\mathbb{Z}$.
links.why: It shows that a discrete valuation ring is a valuation ring whose value group is the integers.

steps: Let $a$ and $b$ be nonzero non-units of a valuation ring $O$.
By the valuation property, $a/b\in O$ or $b/a\in O$; say $a/b\in O$.
Then $a+b=b(1+a/b)$ is a multiple of $b$ in $O$, so it is not a unit.
So the non-units form an ideal, and $O$ is a [local ring](c:local-ring).
links.why: It shows that every valuation ring has a unique maximal ideal.

reminder: A vertex cover of a graph is a set of vertices that contains an endpoint of every edge.
definition: A vertex cover of a [graph](c:graph) $G=(V,E)$ is a set $C\subseteq V$ of [vertices](c:vertex) such that every [edge](c:edge) of $G$ has at least one endpoint in $C$. A minimum vertex cover is a vertex cover with the fewest vertices.
examples: In a triangle on $a$, $b$ and $c$, the set $\{a,b\}$ is a vertex cover, but no single vertex is.
The set of all vertices is always a vertex cover.
In a bipartite graph, the size of a minimum vertex cover equals the size of a maximum [matching](c:matching).
Non-example: in the path $a-b-c-d$, the set $\{b\}$ is not a vertex cover, because the edge $cd$ has no endpoint in it.

reminder: A vertex cut of a graph is a set of vertices whose removal leaves the graph disconnected.
definition: A vertex cut of a [graph](c:graph) $G$ is a set $S$ of [vertices](c:vertex) such that $G-S$ is not a [connected graph](c:connected-graph). For two non-adjacent vertices $u$ and $v$, the set $S$ separates $u$ from $v$ when every $u$-$v$ [path](c:path) meets $S$.
examples: In the path $a-b-c$, the set $\{b\}$ is a vertex cut.
In a cycle $C_n$ with $n\ge4$, any two non-adjacent vertices form a vertex cut.
Menger's theorem says that the least size of a set separating non-adjacent $u$ and $v$ equals the largest number of internally disjoint $u$-$v$ paths.
Non-example: in the complete graph $K_n$, no set of fewer than $n$ vertices is a vertex cut, because the remaining vertices are still pairwise adjacent.

reminder: The Virasoro algebra is the nontrivial central extension of the Witt algebra, with $[L_m,L_n]=(m-n)L_{m+n}+\frac{c}{12}(m^3-m)\delta_{m+n,0}$.
definition: The Virasoro algebra is the [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra) over $\mathbb{C}$ with basis $L_n$ for $n\in\mathbb{Z}$ and a central element $c$, and with bracket $[L_m,L_n]=(m-n)L_{m+n}+\frac{c}{12}(m^3-m)\delta_{m+n,0}$. It is a nontrivial [central extension](c:central-extension) of the Witt algebra, the span of the $L_n$ with $[L_m,L_n]=(m-n)L_{m+n}$. In a representation, $c$ acts as a number, the [central charge](c:central-charge).
examples: The elements $L_{-1}$, $L_0$ and $L_1$ span a copy of $\mathfrak{sl}_2$, because the central term has the factor $m^3-m=0$ for $m=\pm1,0$.
In conformal field theory, the modes $L_n$ of the stress tensor $T(z)=\sum_nL_nz^{-n-2}$ satisfy the Virasoro relations.
Non-example: the Witt algebra, with $[L_m,L_n]=(m-n)L_{m+n}$ and no central term, is the quotient of the Virasoro algebra by $c$, not the Virasoro algebra.

steps: The bracket is bilinear and antisymmetric, because swapping $m$ and $n$ changes the sign of both terms.
The Jacobi identity holds because the term with $m^3-m$ is a $2$-cocycle on the Witt algebra.
So the Virasoro algebra is a [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra).
The special case adds the basis $L_n$, the central element $c$ and this cocycle term.
links.why: It shows what the Virasoro algebra adds to a general Lie algebra: one specific central extension.

reminder: A Waldhausen category is a category with zero object, cofibrations and weak equivalences, where pushouts along cofibrations exist.
definition: A Waldhausen category is a [category](c:category) $C$ with a [zero object](c:has-zero-object) and two classes of morphisms, the [cofibrations](c:cofibration) and the [weak equivalences](c:weak-equivalence), that contain all isomorphisms and are closed under composition. Every map $0\to A$ is a cofibration, and the [pushout](c:pushout) of a cofibration along any map exists and is a cofibration. The gluing lemma holds: a map from a diagram $B\leftarrow A\rightarrowtail A'$ to a diagram $D\leftarrow C\rightarrowtail C'$ that is a weak equivalence at each of the three corners induces a weak equivalence of the pushouts.
examples: Finite pointed CW complexes, with cellular inclusions as cofibrations and weak homotopy equivalences as weak equivalences, form a Waldhausen category.
Bounded chain complexes of finitely generated projective modules, with degreewise split monomorphisms as cofibrations and quasi-isomorphisms as weak equivalences, form a Waldhausen category.
Non-example: the category of sets is not a Waldhausen category, because it has no zero object; the empty set is initial and a point is terminal.

steps: Let $E$ be an [exact category](c:exact-category), an additive category with a class of admissible short exact sequences.
Call a map a cofibration when it is an admissible monomorphism, and a weak equivalence when it is an isomorphism.
Pushouts along admissible monomorphisms exist and are admissible monomorphisms, and isomorphisms pass to pushouts, so the gluing lemma holds.
So $E$ is a Waldhausen category; the general case drops additivity and allows other weak equivalences.
links.why: It shows that a Waldhausen category is an exact category with the extra freedom of weak equivalences.

reminder: A weak equivalence is a morphism of a chosen class that becomes an isomorphism in the localization.
definition: In a [category](c:category) $C$ with a chosen class $W$ of morphisms, the weak equivalences are the elements of $W$, where $W$ contains all isomorphisms and satisfies two-out-of-three. They are the morphisms that the theory treats as isomorphisms: they become invertible in the [localization of the category](c:localization-of-a-category) $C[W^{-1}]$.
examples: In topological spaces, the weak homotopy equivalences are the maps that induce isomorphisms on all [homotopy groups](c:homotopy-group).
In [chain complexes](c:chain-complex), the quasi-isomorphisms are the chain maps that induce isomorphisms on homology.
In any category, the isomorphisms alone form a valid choice of weak equivalences.
Non-example: the inclusion of a point into the circle $S^1$ is not a weak homotopy equivalence, because $\pi_1(S^1)=\mathbb{Z}$ is not zero.

steps: Take any category $C$ and let $W$ be the class of all isomorphisms.
This class is closed under composition and satisfies two-out-of-three.
Inverting isomorphisms changes nothing, so $C[W^{-1}]\simeq C$.
So an [isomorphism](c:isomorphism) is the strictest weak equivalence, and a general $W$ adds more morphisms to invert.
links.why: It shows that weak equivalences relax isomorphisms to the morphisms that a theory wants to invert.

steps: Take $C$ to be the category of topological spaces.
Let $W$ be the maps that induce isomorphisms on all homotopy groups at every basepoint.
This class contains all homotopy equivalences and satisfies two-out-of-three.
So a [weak homotopy equivalence](c:weak-homotopy-equivalence) is a weak equivalence in spaces, and the localization is the homotopy category of spaces.
links.why: It shows the standard example from which the general notion of weak equivalence is abstracted.

steps: Take $C$ to be the category of chain complexes.
Let $W$ be the chain maps that induce isomorphisms on homology in every degree.
This class contains all isomorphisms and satisfies two-out-of-three, because homology is a functor.
So a [quasi-isomorphism](c:quasi-isomorphism) is a weak equivalence of chain complexes, and inverting them gives the derived category.
links.why: It shows that quasi-isomorphisms are the weak equivalences that define the derived category.

reminder: A measure-preserving map $T$ is weakly mixing when the product map $T\times T$ is [ergodic](c:ergodic) on the product space.
definition: A [measure-preserving system](c:measure-preserving-system) $(X,\mu,T)$ with a [probability measure](c:probability-measure) $\mu$ is weakly mixing when $\frac1N\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}|\mu(T^{-n}A\cap B)-\mu(A)\mu(B)|\to0$ as $N\to\infty$, for all measurable sets $A$ and $B$. Equivalently, $T\times T$ is [ergodic](c:ergodic) on $X\times X$.
examples: Every [Bernoulli scheme](c:bernoulli-scheme) is mixing, so it is weakly mixing.
The doubling map $x\mapsto2x\bmod1$ with Lebesgue measure is mixing, so it is weakly mixing.
Non-example: the rotation $x\mapsto x+\alpha\bmod1$ by an irrational $\alpha$ is ergodic but not weakly mixing, because $f(x)=e^{2\pi ix}$ satisfies $f\circ T=e^{2\pi i\alpha}f$.

steps: Let $T$ be weakly mixing and let $A$ be a measurable set with $T^{-1}A=A$.
Then $T^{-n}A\cap A=A$ for all $n$, so each term $|\mu(T^{-n}A\cap A)-\mu(A)^2|$ equals $\mu(A)-\mu(A)^2$.
The averages tend to $0$, so $\mu(A)=\mu(A)^2$ and $\mu(A)\in\{0,1\}$.
So $T$ is [ergodic](c:ergodic), and weak mixing adds the decay of correlations for all pairs of sets.
links.why: It shows that weak mixing is ergodicity with a stronger condition on pairs of sets.

reminder: An object $I$ is weakly initial when there is at least one morphism from $I$ to every object.
definition: An object $I$ of a [category](c:category) is weakly initial when, for every object $X$, there exists at least one morphism $I\to X$. An [initial object](c:initial-object) is the case where this morphism is also unique.
examples: Every initial object is weakly initial.
In the category of nonempty sets, a one-point set is weakly initial, because each nonempty set has an element to map to; it is not initial, because the choice is not unique.
In a poset viewed as a category, an object is weakly initial exactly when it is a least element.
Non-example: the category of fields has no weakly initial object, because a field homomorphism preserves the characteristic, so no field maps to fields of every characteristic.

steps: Let $I$ be an [initial object](c:initial-object), so there is exactly one morphism $I\to X$ for every object $X$.
Exactly one morphism is at least one morphism.
So $I$ is weakly initial.
A weakly initial object drops the uniqueness condition.
links.why: It shows that weak initiality is initiality without uniqueness of the morphisms.

reminder: For $[Q,P]=i\hbar$, the unitary groups $e^{isQ}$ and $e^{itP}$ commute up to the phase $e^{-i\hbar st}$.
definition: Let $Q$ and $P$ be self-adjoint operators on a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) with the [canonical commutation relation](c:canonical-commutation-relation) $[Q,P]=i\hbar$. The Weyl relations are the relations $U(s)V(t)=e^{-i\hbar st}V(t)U(s)$ for all real $s$ and $t$ between the [unitary](c:unitary-operator) groups $U(s)=e^{isQ}$ and $V(t)=e^{itP}$. They define the [Weyl algebra](c:weyl-algebra).
examples: On $L^2(\mathbb{R})$ with $Q$ multiplication by $x$ and $P=-i\hbar\,d/dx$, the groups are $(U(s)\psi)(x)=e^{isx}\psi(x)$ and $(V(t)\psi)(x)=\psi(x+\hbar t)$, and they satisfy the Weyl relations.
The Stone-von Neumann theorem says that every irreducible regular representation of the Weyl relations is unitarily equivalent to this one.
Non-example: the relation $QP-PQ=i\hbar$ itself is not a Weyl relation, because it cannot hold for bounded operators, which is why one passes to exponentials.

reminder: White noise is a stochastic process of uncorrelated random variables with mean zero and the same finite variance.
definition: A discrete-time white noise is a [stochastic process](c:stochastic-process) $(X_t)$ of [random variables](c:random-variable) with [expected value](c:expected-value) $0$, the same finite [variance](c:variance) $\sigma^2$ for all $t$, and no correlation between different times, that is, $\mathrm{E}[X_sX_t]=0$ for $s\neq t$. Its power spectrum is flat, so all frequencies carry the same power.
examples: A sequence of independent [normal](c:normal-distribution) variables with mean $0$ and variance $\sigma^2$ is Gaussian white noise.
Independent fair coin flips with the values $+1$ and $-1$ form white noise.

Non-example: the random walk $S_n=\varepsilon_1+\cdots+\varepsilon_n$ of white noise $\varepsilon_i$ is not white noise, because $\operatorname{Var}S_n=n\sigma^2$ grows and $S_n$ and $S_{n+1}$ are correlated.

steps: Let $(X_t)$ be white noise with variance $\sigma^2$.
Its mean is $0$ at every time, so the mean does not depend on $t$.
Its covariance is $\sigma^2$ at lag $0$ and $0$ at every other lag, so it depends only on the lag.
So white noise is a weakly [stationary process](c:stationary-process) with the extra property that its values are uncorrelated.
links.why: It shows that results for weakly stationary processes, such as spectral theory, apply to white noise.

reminder: The Whitney trick removes two intersection points of opposite sign by pushing one submanifold across an embedded Whitney disc.
definition: Let $A$ and $B$ be submanifolds of complementary dimension in a [manifold](c:manifold) $M$ of dimension at least $5$, with a [transversal](c:transversality) intersection that contains two points $p$ and $q$ of opposite sign. Suppose that arcs of $A$ and $B$ from $p$ to $q$ bound an embedded $2$-disc, the Whitney disc, whose interior misses $A$ and $B$. Then an [isotopy](c:isotopy) of $A$ near this disc removes $p$ and $q$ and leaves the other intersection points unchanged.
examples: In the proof of the [h-cobordism](c:h-cobordism) theorem, the trick lowers the geometric intersection number of two handle spheres to the algebraic one, which lets the handles cancel.
Whitney used it to remove pairs of double points of an immersion, in his proof that a smooth $n$-manifold with $n\ge3$ embeds in $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$.
Non-example: two intersection points of the same sign cannot be removed by this trick, because the algebraic intersection number does not change under isotopy.
Non-example: in a smooth $4$-manifold, the Whitney disc may fail to be embedded, so the trick can fail.

reminder: Wick rotation replaces real time $t$ by imaginary time $t=-i\tau$ to turn a Lorentzian quantity into a Euclidean one.
definition: Wick rotation is the [analytic continuation](c:analytic-continuation) of a quantity from real time $t$ to imaginary time $t=-i\tau$ with $\tau$ real. It changes the [Minkowski metric](c:minkowski-metric) $-dt^2+d\vec{x}^2$ into the Euclidean metric $d\tau^2+d\vec{x}^2$, and so it turns a relativistic field theory into a Euclidean field theory with [complex numbers](c:complex-number) as the bridge.
examples: The oscillating factor $e^{-itH/\hbar}$ becomes the damped factor $e^{-\tau H/\hbar}$, so the Schrödinger propagator becomes the [heat kernel](c:heat-kernel).
In the [path integral](c:path-integral), the weight $e^{iS}$ becomes the weight $e^{-S_E}$ with the Euclidean action $S_E$.
Wightman functions, continued to imaginary times, give the Schwinger functions of Euclidean field theory.
Non-example: the real rescaling $t=2\tau$ changes the unit of time but keeps the Lorentzian signature, so it is not a Wick rotation.

steps: Take a function $f(t)$ that is analytic in a region of the complex $t$-plane that contains the real axis.
Continue $f$ analytically along the rotation $t=e^{-i\theta}s$ with $\theta$ from $0$ to $\pi/2$.
The end of the rotation is the imaginary axis $t=-i\tau$.
So a Wick rotation is an [analytic continuation](c:analytic-continuation) in time by a quarter turn from the real axis to the imaginary axis.
links.why: It shows that Wick rotation is analytic continuation, so it needs analyticity in the rotation region.

reminder: The growth of a group counts the elements that are products of at most $n$ generators, as $n$ grows.
definition: Let $G$ be a [finitely generated group](c:finitely-generated-group) with a finite generating set $S$ that is closed under inverses. The growth function $\gamma_S(n)$ is the number of elements of $G$ that are products of at most $n$ elements of $S$. The growth of $G$ is the rate at which $\gamma_S(n)$ grows, and it does not depend on $S$ up to the usual equivalence of growth rates.
examples: In $\mathbb{Z}^d$ with the standard generators, $\gamma(n)$ grows like $n^d$, which is polynomial growth.
In the [free group](c:free-group) $F_2$ on two generators, $\gamma(n)=2\cdot3^n-1$, so the growth is exponential.
Grigorchuk's group has intermediate growth, faster than every polynomial and slower than every exponential.
Non-example: the additive group $\mathbb{Q}$ is not finitely generated, so it has no growth function, because every generating set is infinite and gives infinite balls.

reminder: The Wronskian of $n$ functions is the determinant of the matrix of the functions and their derivatives up to order $n-1$.
definition: The Wronskian of $n$ functions $f_1,\dots,f_n$ with $n-1$ [derivatives](c:derivative) is the [determinant](c:determinant) of the $n\times n$ [matrix](c:matrix) whose $i$-th row holds the derivatives of order $i-1$, that is, $W(f_1,\dots,f_n)(x)=\det\bigl(f_j^{(i-1)}(x)\bigr)_{i,j=1}^n$. It is a function of $x$.
examples: For the functions $\cos$ and $\sin$, $W=\cos^2+\sin^2=1$.
For the functions $1$, $x$ and $x^2$, $W=2$.
For $e^{ax}$ and $e^{bx}$, $W=(b-a)e^{(a+b)x}$.
Non-example: the determinant of the values $f_j(x_i)$ at $n$ distinct points uses no derivatives, so it is not the Wronskian.

reminder: The Yoneda embedding sends each object $X$ of a locally small category to the representable presheaf $\mathrm{Hom}(-,X)$.
definition: For a [locally small](c:locally-small) category $C$, the Yoneda embedding is the [functor](c:functor) $y:C\to[C^{op},\mathrm{Set}]$ into the [category of presheaves](c:category-of-presheaves) with $y(X)=\mathrm{Hom}_C(-,X)$ on objects and $y(f)=f\circ-$ on morphisms. By the Yoneda lemma, it is a [full and faithful functor](c:full-and-faithful-functor), and each $y(X)$ is a representable [presheaf](c:presheaf).
examples: For a poset $P$, the presheaf $y(p)$ is the down-set $\{q\mid q\le p\}$, so $P$ embeds in its down-sets.
For a monoid $M$ viewed as a one-object category, $y$ sends $m$ to the map $x\mapsto mx$ on $M$, which is Cayley's embedding.
Non-example: on the category with one object and only the identity, presheaves are sets, and a two-element set is not isomorphic to $y(*)$, which is a one-point set.

steps: The Yoneda embedding $y$ sends a morphism $f:X\to Y$ to the natural transformation $f\circ-:y(X)\to y(Y)$.
By the Yoneda lemma, natural transformations $y(X)\to y(Y)$ correspond bijectively to elements of $y(Y)(X)=\mathrm{Hom}(X,Y)$.
This bijection inverts the action of $y$ on morphisms, so $y$ is full and faithful.
So $y$ is a [full and faithful functor](c:full-and-faithful-functor) with the special target $[C^{op},\mathrm{Set}]$.
links.why: It shows that the Yoneda embedding identifies a category with a full subcategory of its presheaves.

reminder: The zero locus of a function is the set of points where the function takes the value zero.
definition: For a [function](c:function) $f:X\to R$ into a set $R$ with a [zero](c:zero), the zero locus is $Z(f)=\{x\in X\mid f(x)=0\}$, the [preimage](c:preimage) of $0$. For a family of functions $f_i$, the zero locus is the set $\bigcap_iZ(f_i)$ of their common zeros.
examples: The zero locus of $x^2+y^2-1$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$ is the unit circle.
The zero locus of $xy$ is the union of the two coordinate axes, and the zero locus of the pair $x$ and $y$ is the origin.
The zero locus of $\sin$ on $\mathbb{R}$ is the set $\pi\mathbb{Z}$.
Non-example: the set of points where $f(x)\neq0$ is the complement of the zero locus, not the zero locus.

steps: A [level set](c:level-set) of $f$ at the value $c$ is the preimage $f^{-1}(c)$.
Take the value $c=0$ in a codomain that has a zero.
Then the preimage $f^{-1}(0)$ is exactly the zero locus $Z(f)$.
So a zero locus is a level set at $0$, and every level set $f^{-1}(c)$ is the zero locus of $f-c$ when subtraction exists.
links.why: It shows that zero loci and level sets are the same idea, up to a shift of the value.

steps: Take a field $k$ and polynomials $f_1,\dots,f_m$ in $k[x_1,\dots,x_n]$, viewed as functions $k^n\to k$.
Their zero locus $Z(f_1,\dots,f_m)\subseteq k^n$ is an algebraic set.
An [affine variety](c:affine-variety) is such a zero locus, usually required to be irreducible.
So algebraic geometry is the case where the functions are polynomials.
links.why: It shows that an affine variety is a zero locus of polynomials, so zero-locus tools apply to it.

reminder: A 2-category has objects, morphisms and 2-morphisms, with composition that is strictly associative and unital.
definition: A 2-category is a [category enriched](c:enriched-category) in the category of small categories: it has objects, $1$-morphisms between objects, and $2$-morphisms between parallel $1$-morphisms. The composition of $1$-morphisms and the vertical and horizontal compositions of $2$-morphisms are strictly associative and unital and satisfy the interchange law.
examples: The category $\mathbf{Cat}$ of small categories has functors as $1$-morphisms and [natural transformations](c:natural-transformation) as $2$-morphisms.
A strict monoidal category is a $2$-category with one object.
Non-example: the bicategory of spans of sets composes by pullback, and its composition is associative only up to isomorphism, so it is not a $2$-category.

steps: A [bicategory](c:bicategory) has composition that is associative and unital only up to invertible $2$-morphisms, the associators and unitors.
In a $2$-category, these associators and unitors are all identity $2$-morphisms.
The coherence conditions of a bicategory then hold trivially.
So every $2$-category is a bicategory, and the special case adds strict associativity and unit laws.
links.why: It shows that a 2-category is a bicategory with all coherence isomorphisms made trivial.

steps: Let $C$ be a [category](c:category).
Take the objects of $C$, and take its morphisms as the $1$-morphisms.
Add one $2$-morphism, the identity, from each morphism to itself.
The $2$-category axioms hold, so $C$ is a $2$-category with only identity $2$-morphisms.
links.why: It shows that every ordinary category is a 2-category in which 2-morphisms carry no information.

reminder: A graph is 2-edge-connected when it is connected and has no bridge, so removing any one edge leaves it connected.
definition: A [graph](c:graph) $G$ is 2-edge-connected when it is a [connected graph](c:connected-graph) and removing any single [edge](c:edge) leaves a connected graph. Equivalently, $G$ is connected and has no bridge, where a bridge is an edge whose removal disconnects the graph.
examples: Every cycle $C_n$ with $n\ge3$ is 2-edge-connected.
The complete graph $K_n$ with $n\ge3$ is 2-edge-connected.
By Robbins' theorem, a graph is 2-edge-connected exactly when it has a strongly connected orientation.
Non-example: the path $a-b-c$ is connected, but removing the edge $ab$ disconnects it, so it is not 2-edge-connected.

steps: Take a 2-edge-connected graph $G$.
By definition, $G$ is a [connected graph](c:connected-graph).
The extra condition is that no edge of $G$ is a bridge.
So the 2-edge-connected graphs are the connected graphs that have no bridge.
links.why: It shows that 2-edge-connectivity is connectivity that survives the loss of any one edge.

reminder: A 3-cycle is a permutation that sends $a\mapsto b\mapsto c\mapsto a$ and fixes every other element.
definition: A 3-cycle is a [permutation](c:permutation) $(a\ b\ c)$ of a set that sends $a$ to $b$, $b$ to $c$ and $c$ to $a$ for three distinct elements, and fixes all other elements. It has order $3$ and it is an even permutation.
examples: In $S_3$, the 3-cycles are $(1\ 2\ 3)$ and $(1\ 3\ 2)$, and they are inverse to each other.
Each 3-cycle is a product of two [transpositions](c:transposition), for example $(1\ 2\ 3)=(1\ 3)(1\ 2)$ when maps compose from right to left.
The alternating group $A_n$ with $n\ge3$ is generated by the 3-cycles.
Non-example: $(1\ 2)(3\ 4)$ and $(1\ 2\ 3\ 4)$ are not 3-cycles, because the first has two cycles of length $2$ and the second has one cycle of length $4$.

steps: A [cycle](c:cycle-of-a-permutation) of length $k$ sends $a_1\mapsto a_2\mapsto\cdots\mapsto a_k\mapsto a_1$ and fixes every other element.
Take the case $k=3$ in this definition.
Then the cycle sends $a_1\mapsto a_2\mapsto a_3\mapsto a_1$.
So a 3-cycle is a cycle of length $3$.
links.why: It shows that a 3-cycle is the cycle of length three, so cycle facts apply to it.

reminder: An $A_\infty$-ring is a ring whose multiplication is associative up to a coherent system of higher homotopies.
definition: An $A_\infty$-ring is a [monoid](c:monoid-in-a-monoidal-infinity-1-category) in a monoidal [stable (infinity,1)-category](c:stable-infinity-1-category), typically the category of spectra with the smash product. So it is an object $R$ with a unit and a multiplication $R\otimes R\to R$ that are associative and unital up to a coherent system of higher homotopies.
examples: The Eilenberg-MacLane spectrum $HR$ of an ordinary [ring](c:ring) $R$ is an $A_\infty$-ring.
The sphere spectrum $S$ and the K-theory spectra $KU$ and $KO$ are $A_\infty$-rings, and they are even $E_\infty$-rings.
Non-example: a spectrum with a multiplication that is associative only up to homotopy is a homotopy ring spectrum; it is not an $A_\infty$-ring until higher homotopies are chosen.

steps: Let $R$ be an [E-infinity ring](c:e-infinity-ring), whose multiplication is associative and commutative up to coherent homotopy.
Forget the commutativity data and keep the associativity data.
The result is an $A_\infty$-ring.
So an $E_\infty$-ring is an $A_\infty$-ring with commutativity data added.
links.why: It shows that every theorem about A-infinity rings also holds for E-infinity rings.

steps: Let $R$ be an ordinary [ring](c:ring).
Its Eilenberg-MacLane spectrum $HR$ has a multiplication that is associative with all higher coherences, because the product of $R$ is strictly associative.
So $HR$ is an $A_\infty$-ring.
Thus rings are the discrete $A_\infty$-rings, whose homotopy groups sit in degree $0$.
links.why: It shows that an A-infinity ring is a ring that is allowed to have higher homotopy groups.

reminder: An abelian integral is the integral of a rational differential $R(x,y)\,dx$ on an algebraic curve $F(x,y)=0$.
definition: An abelian integral is an integral $\int R(x,y)\,dx$, where $R$ is a rational function and $y$ is an algebraic function of $x$ given by $F(x,y)=0$. On the [algebraic curve](c:algebraic-curve) $F=0$, seen as a [compact Riemann surface](c:compact-riemann-surface), it is a [line integral](c:line-integral) of the [meromorphic](c:meromorphic-function) differential $\omega=R(x,y)\,dx$, and its value depends on the chosen path.
examples: The integral $\int dx/\sqrt{1-x^2}=\arcsin x$ is an abelian integral on the curve $y^2=1-x^2$ of genus $0$.
The integral $\int dx/\sqrt{x^3+ax+b}$ is an elliptic integral, an abelian integral on a curve of genus $1$.
On the curve $y^2=f(x)$ with $f$ of degree $5$ and no repeated roots, which has genus $2$, the integrals $\int dx/y$ and $\int x\,dx/y$ have no poles.
Non-example: the integral $\int e^{x^2}\,dx$ is not abelian, because $e^{x^2}$ is not a rational function of $x$ and an algebraic function $y$.

steps: Take the algebraic curve $F(x,y)=0$ as a Riemann surface $C$.
The expression $R(x,y)\,dx$ is a meromorphic $1$-form $\omega$ on $C$.
Choose a path $\gamma$ on $C$ that avoids the poles of $\omega$.
Then $\int_\gamma\omega$ is a [line integral](c:line-integral), and it is the abelian integral along $\gamma$.
links.why: It shows that abelian integrals are line integrals of rational forms, so their values depend on the path.

reminder: A group is acyclic when its classifying space has the same homology as a point.
definition: A [discrete group](c:discrete-group) $\Gamma$ is acyclic when its [classifying space](c:classifying-space) $B\Gamma$ has the [homology](c:ordinary-homology) of a point, that is, $H_n(B\Gamma;\mathbb{Z})=0$ for every $n>0$. Then the map $B\Gamma\to*$ is a homology equivalence.
examples: The trivial group is acyclic.
Higman's group, with four generators and four relations, is acyclic.
The group of compactly supported homeomorphisms of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is acyclic, by a theorem of Mather.
Non-example: $\mathbb{Z}$ is not acyclic, because $B\mathbb{Z}\simeq S^1$ and $H_1(S^1;\mathbb{Z})=\mathbb{Z}$.

steps: The group $H_1(\Gamma;\mathbb{Z})$ is the abelianization $\Gamma/[\Gamma,\Gamma]$.
An acyclic group has $H_1(\Gamma;\mathbb{Z})=0$.
So $\Gamma=[\Gamma,\Gamma]$, which means that $\Gamma$ is a [perfect group](c:is-perfect).
Acyclicity adds the condition that all higher homology groups also vanish.
links.why: It shows that an acyclic group is a perfect group whose higher homology also vanishes.

reminder: The Adams-Novikov spectral sequence is the Adams spectral sequence that is based on complex cobordism $MU$.
definition: For a spectrum $X$, the Adams-Novikov spectral sequence is the $E$-based [Adams spectral sequence](c:adams-spectral-sequence) with $E=MU$, the spectrum of [complex cobordism](c:complex-cobordism). Its $E_2$-page is $\operatorname{Ext}^{s,t}_{MU_*MU}(MU_*,MU_*X)$, computed with [Ext](c:ext), and under suitable conditions on $X$ it converges to $\pi_{t-s}X$.
examples: For the sphere spectrum, the $E_2$-page is $\operatorname{Ext}_{MU_*MU}(MU_*,MU_*)$, and the sequence converges to the stable homotopy groups of spheres.
The pair $(MU_*,MU_*MU)$ is the Hopf algebroid of formal group laws and their strict isomorphisms, so the $E_2$-page is a formal-group computation.
Non-example: the classical Adams spectral sequence uses $E=H\mathbb{F}_p$ and has $E_2$ given by Ext over the Steenrod algebra, so it is a different $E$-Adams spectral sequence.

steps: Fix a ring spectrum $E$ and form the $E$-based Adams resolution of $X$.
Its $E_2$-page is an Ext group of $E_*E$-comodules whenever $E_*E$ is flat over $E_*$.
Take $E=MU$, for which $MU_*MU$ is flat over $MU_*$.
The result is the Adams-Novikov spectral sequence, the $MU$ case of the [Adams spectral sequence](c:adams-spectral-sequence).
links.why: It shows that the Adams-Novikov spectral sequence is the Adams spectral sequence for a different choice of base theory.

reminder: An additive content is a set function with value zero on the empty set that adds over finite disjoint unions.
definition: Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a [family of sets](c:family-of-sets) of subsets of a set $X$, such as a [semiring of sets](c:is-set-semiring). An additive content on $\mathcal{C}$ is a function $m:\mathcal{C}\to[0,\infty]$ with $m(\varnothing)=0$ and $m(\bigcup_iA_i)=\sum_im(A_i)$ for every finite family of pairwise disjoint sets $A_i\in\mathcal{C}$ whose union lies in $\mathcal{C}$. More generally, $m$ may take values in an additive commutative monoid.
examples: On the half-open intervals $[a,b)$ of $\mathbb{R}$, the length $m([a,b))=b-a$ is an additive content.
Every [measure](c:measure), restricted to any family of measurable sets, is an additive content.
On the finite subsets of an infinite set, the counting function $m(A)=|A|$ is an additive content.
Non-example: the function $m(A)=|A|^2$ on finite sets is not additive, because $m(\{a,b\})=4$ but $m(\{a\})+m(\{b\})=2$.

steps: Let $\mu$ be a [measure](c:measure) on a $\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal{A}$ and let $\mathcal{C}$ be any family of sets in $\mathcal{A}$.
Then $\mu(\varnothing)=0$ by the definition of a measure.
Countable additivity gives finite additivity, because a finite disjoint family can be padded with empty sets.
So the restriction of $\mu$ to $\mathcal{C}$ is an additive content, and a content need not be countably additive.
links.why: It shows that every measure gives contents, and that a content is a measure without countable additivity.

reminder: The ADM mass is the total mass of an asymptotically flat space, read from the metric at infinity.
definition: Let $(M,g)$ be an [asymptotically flat](c:asymptotically-flat-manifold) [Riemannian manifold](c:riemannian-manifold) of dimension $3$, the initial slice of a [spacetime](c:spacetime), with coordinates $x^i$ near infinity. Its ADM mass is $m=\frac{1}{16\pi}\lim_{r\to\infty}\int_{S_r}(\partial_jg_{ij}-\partial_ig_{jj})\,\nu^i\,dA$, a [surface integral](c:surface-integral) over the coordinate sphere $S_r$ with outward unit normal $\nu$, in units with $G=c=1$.
examples: A slice $t=\mathrm{const}$ of the Schwarzschild spacetime of mass $m$ has ADM mass $m$.
Flat $\mathbb{R}^3$ has ADM mass $0$.
The positive energy theorem says that the ADM mass is nonnegative when the scalar curvature is nonnegative.
Non-example: a compact Riemannian $3$-manifold has no asymptotic end, so it has no ADM mass.

reminder: The affine line over a field $k$ is the affine scheme with coordinate ring $k[t]$, whose $k$-points are the elements of $k$.
definition: The affine line over a [field](c:field) $k$ is the [affine scheme](c:affine-scheme) $\mathbb{A}^1_k=\operatorname{Spec}k[t]$ of the [polynomial ring](c:polynomial-ring) in one variable. Its functor of points sends a $k$-algebra $R$ to the underlying set of $R$, so its $k$-points are the elements of $k$.
examples: The scheme $\mathbb{A}^1_{\mathbb{C}}$ has the complex numbers as closed points, and one generic point $(0)$.
Morphisms from a $k$-scheme $X$ to $\mathbb{A}^1_k$ are the global functions on $X$.
Over $\mathbb{F}_p$, the $\mathbb{F}_p$-points of $\mathbb{A}^1$ are the $p$ elements of $\mathbb{F}_p$.
Non-example: the projective line $\mathbb{P}^1_k$ adds a point at infinity, and it is not affine, because its only global functions are the constants.

steps: Let $A=k[t]$, a commutative ring.
Then $\operatorname{Spec}A$ is an [affine scheme](c:affine-scheme) by definition.
This affine scheme is the affine line $\mathbb{A}^1_k$.
So the affine line is the affine scheme of the polynomial ring in one variable.
links.why: It shows that the affine line is one affine scheme, so the tools for affine schemes apply to it.

steps: Affine $n$-space over $k$ has the set $k^n$ as its $k$-points and the ring $k[t_1,\dots,t_n]$ as its coordinate ring.
Take the case $n=1$ in this definition.
Then the points form the set $k^1=k$, and the coordinate ring is $k[t]$.
So the affine line is [affine space](c:affine-space) of dimension $1$.
links.why: It shows that the affine line is the one-dimensional case of affine space.

reminder: An affine monoid is a finitely generated commutative monoid that embeds in $\mathbb{Z}^d$ for some $d$.
definition: An affine monoid is a finitely generated submonoid of the [abelian group](c:abelian-group) $\mathbb{Z}^d$ for some $d$. Equivalently, it is a finitely generated commutative cancellative [monoid](c:monoid) whose group of differences has no torsion.
examples: The monoid $\mathbb{N}^d$ of lattice points with nonnegative coordinates is an affine monoid.
The numerical semigroup generated by $2$ and $3$, namely $\{0,2,3,4,\dots\}$, is an affine monoid in $\mathbb{N}$.
By Gordan's lemma, the lattice points of a rational polyhedral cone form an affine monoid.
Non-example: the monoid $(\mathbb{Q}_{\ge0},+)$ is not finitely generated, and the group $(\mathbb{Z}/2,+)$ does not embed in $\mathbb{Z}^d$, because it has torsion.

steps: Take a submonoid $M$ of $\mathbb{Z}^d$.
It contains $0$ and is closed under addition, so it is a [monoid](c:monoid).
Addition in $\mathbb{Z}^d$ is commutative, so $M$ is a commutative monoid.
The affine case adds the condition that $M$ is finitely generated.
links.why: It shows that an affine monoid is a commutative monoid with finiteness and torsion-free conditions.

reminder: The affine plane over a field $k$ is the set $k^2$ with the polynomials in two variables as its coordinate ring.
definition: The affine plane over a [field](c:field) $k$ is $\mathbb{A}^2_k$, the set $k^2$ of pairs $(x,y)$ with the [polynomial ring](c:polynomial-ring) $k[x,y]$ as its ring of functions. A plane curve is the [zero locus](c:zero-locus) of a polynomial $f(x,y)$.
examples: The plane $\mathbb{A}^2_{\mathbb{R}}$ is the real plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ with its polynomial functions.
The parabola $y=x^2$ is the zero locus of the polynomial $y-x^2$ in $\mathbb{A}^2_k$.
The Abhyankar-Moh theorem says that every embedding of the affine line into $\mathbb{A}^2_{\mathbb{C}}$ is a coordinate line after an automorphism of the plane.
Non-example: the projective plane $\mathbb{P}^2_k$ adds a line at infinity, so it is not an affine plane.

steps: Affine $n$-space over $k$ has the set $k^n$ as its $k$-points and the ring $k[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ as its coordinate ring.
Take the case $n=2$ in this definition.
Then the points are the pairs $(x,y)\in k^2$, and the coordinate ring is $k[x,y]$.
So the affine plane is [affine space](c:affine-space) of dimension $2$.
links.why: It shows that the affine plane is the two-dimensional case of affine space.

reminder: An affine scheme is a locally ringed space isomorphic to the spectrum $\operatorname{Spec}A$ of a commutative ring $A$.
definition: An affine scheme is a [locally ringed space](c:locally-ringed-space) that is isomorphic to $\operatorname{Spec}A$ for some commutative [ring](c:ring) $A$. Here $\operatorname{Spec}A$ is the [spectrum of the ring](c:spectrum-of-a-commutative-ring): the prime ideals of $A$ with the Zariski topology and the sheaf of localizations of $A$. The ring $A$ is recovered as the ring of global functions.
examples: The spectrum $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb{Z}$ is an affine scheme, and so is $\operatorname{Spec}k$ for a field $k$, which is a single point.
The affine space $\mathbb{A}^n_k=\operatorname{Spec}k[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ is an affine scheme.
The scheme $\operatorname{Spec}k[x]/(x^2)$ is an affine scheme: a point with a nilpotent function.
Non-example: the plane minus the origin, $\mathbb{A}^2_k\setminus\{0\}$, is a scheme but is not affine, because every function on it extends to the whole plane.

steps: Let $V\subseteq k^n$ be an [affine variety](c:affine-variety) with coordinate ring $k[V]=k[x_1,\dots,x_n]/I(V)$.
The ring $k[V]$ is a commutative ring.
So $\operatorname{Spec}k[V]$ is an affine scheme, and for an algebraically closed field $k$ its closed points are the points of $V$.
An affine scheme extends this construction to all commutative rings, and it allows nilpotents and non-closed points.
links.why: It shows that an affine scheme is an affine variety with the restrictions on the ring removed.

steps: A [scheme](c:scheme) is a locally ringed space that has an open cover by affine schemes.
Let $X$ be an affine scheme and cover $X$ by the single open set $X$.
Then $X$ has an open cover by affine schemes, so $X$ is a scheme.
The affine case adds the condition that one open set is enough to cover.
links.why: It shows that an affine scheme is a scheme that is its own affine chart.

reminder: A $k$-affinoid space is the space $\operatorname{Sp}A$ of a quotient $A$ of a Tate algebra over a complete non-Archimedean field $k$.
definition: Let $k$ be a complete non-Archimedean field. A $k$-affinoid algebra is a quotient of a [Tate algebra](c:tate-algebra) $k\langle T_1,\dots,T_n\rangle$, the [power series](c:power-series) whose coefficients tend to $0$, by an ideal. A $k$-affinoid space $\operatorname{Sp}A$ is the object that corresponds to a $k$-affinoid algebra $A$ in the [opposite category](c:opposite-category), and its points are the maximal ideals of $A$.
examples: The closed unit disc $\operatorname{Sp}k\langle T\rangle$ is a $k$-affinoid space.
The closed polydisc $\operatorname{Sp}k\langle T_1,\dots,T_n\rangle$ is a $k$-affinoid space.
For $a\in k$ with $a\neq0$, the closed disc $\{|t|\le|a|\}$ is the space $\operatorname{Sp}k\langle T/a\rangle$.
Non-example: the open unit disc $\{|t|<1\}$ is not affinoid, because it is an increasing union of closed discs of smaller radius, and it is not $\operatorname{Sp}A$ for any affinoid algebra $A$.

reminder: An algebra over an operad $P$ is an object with maps $P(n)\otimes A^{\otimes n}\to A$ that respect the operad structure.
definition: Let $P$ be an [operad](c:operad) in a [symmetric monoidal category](c:symmetric-monoidal-category) $C$. A $P$-algebra is an object $A$ of $C$ with maps $P(n)\otimes A^{\otimes n}\to A$ for all $n$ that are equivariant for the actions of the [symmetric groups](c:symmetric-group) and compatible with the composition and the unit of $P$. Equivalently, it is a morphism of operads from $P$ to the endomorphism operad of $A$.
examples: Algebras over the associative operad are associative algebras, that is, monoids in $C$.
Algebras over the commutative operad are commutative algebras, and algebras over the Lie operad are Lie algebras.
Non-example: the cross product on $\mathbb{R}^3$ is not associative, so it is not an algebra over the associative operad, although it is an algebra over the Lie operad.

steps: Take the [associative operad](c:associative-operad), whose operations are the ordered products of $n$ inputs.
An algebra over it has one binary product $\mu:A\otimes A\to A$, the image of the product $x_1x_2$.
The operad relation $(x_1x_2)x_3=x_1(x_2x_3)$ says that $\mu$ is associative.
So algebras over the associative operad are the [associative algebras](c:associative-algebra).
links.why: It shows that an associative algebra is an algebra over one particular operad.

steps: Take the [Lie operad](c:lie-operad), which is generated by one antisymmetric binary operation.
An algebra over it has one binary bracket $[\,,]:A\otimes A\to A$ that is antisymmetric.
The relations of the Lie operad say that the bracket satisfies the Jacobi identity.
So algebras over the Lie operad are the [Lie algebras](c:lie-algebra).
links.why: It shows that a Lie algebra is an algebra over one particular operad.

steps: Take the commutative operad, whose operations are the products of $n$ inputs in no particular order.
An algebra over it has one binary product $\mu:A\otimes A\to A$.
The operad relations say that $\mu$ is associative and commutative.
So algebras over the commutative operad are the [commutative algebras](c:commutative-algebra).
links.why: It shows that a commutative algebra is an algebra over one particular operad.

reminder: A smooth projective variety has an ample canonical bundle when some positive power of that bundle is very ample.
definition: Let $X$ be a smooth [projective variety](c:projective-variety) of dimension $n$, and let $K_X$ be its [canonical bundle](c:canonical-bundle), the bundle of $n$-forms. The canonical bundle is ample when $K_X^{\otimes m}$ is a [very ample line bundle](c:very-ample-line-bundle) for some $m>0$, so that sections of this power embed $X$ in a projective space.
examples: A smooth curve of genus $g\ge2$ has $\deg K=2g-2>0$, so its canonical bundle is ample.
A smooth hypersurface of degree $d\ge n+3$ in $\mathbb{P}^{n+1}$ has $K=\mathcal{O}(d-n-2)$, which is ample.
Non-example: projective space $\mathbb{P}^n$ has $K=\mathcal{O}(-n-1)$, which is anti-ample, and an elliptic curve has $K\cong\mathcal{O}$, which is trivial; neither is ample.

steps: A line bundle $L$ is [ample](c:ample-sheaf) when some power $L^{\otimes m}$ with $m>0$ is very ample.
Among the line bundles on $X$, single out the canonical bundle $K_X$.
If $K_X$ is ample, then $X$ has an ample canonical bundle.
So this is the case $L=K_X$ of ampleness, and it embeds $X$ by the sections of $K_X^{\otimes m}$ for $m$ large.
links.why: It shows that an ample canonical bundle is ampleness applied to one specific line bundle.

reminder: An analytic space is a space that is locally the zero locus of finitely many analytic functions, with their ideal divided out.
definition: A complex analytic space is a [locally ringed space](c:locally-ringed-space) $(X,\mathcal{O}_X)$ that is locally isomorphic to a model $(Z,\mathcal{O}_U/I)$. Here $U\subseteq\mathbb{C}^n$ is open, $\mathcal{O}_U$ is the sheaf of [holomorphic functions](c:holomorphic-function) on $U$, $I$ is the ideal sheaf generated by finitely many holomorphic functions $f_1,\dots,f_k$, and $Z$ is their [zero locus](c:zero-locus).
examples: Every [complex manifold](c:complex-manifold) is an analytic space.
The cusp $\{y^2=x^3\}\subset\mathbb{C}^2$ with the sheaf $\mathcal{O}/(y^2-x^3)$ is an analytic space with a singular point.
The point $\{0\}\subset\mathbb{C}$ with the sheaf $\mathcal{O}/(x^2)$ is an analytic space with a nilpotent function.
Non-example: the real line with its sheaf of smooth functions is not an analytic space, because smooth functions are not locally given by convergent power series.

steps: Let $M$ be a [complex manifold](c:complex-manifold), so each point has a chart onto an open set $U\subseteq\mathbb{C}^n$.
Take the model with no equations, $k=0$, so that $I=0$ and $Z=U$.
Then $M$ is locally isomorphic to $(U,\mathcal{O}_U)$, so $M$ is an analytic space.
A general analytic space allows equations in the local model, so it can have singular points.
links.why: It shows that analytic spaces extend complex manifolds to spaces with singularities.

steps: The stalks of $\mathcal{O}_U/I$ are quotients of the local rings of convergent power series.
A quotient of a local ring by a proper ideal is a local ring.
So each model is a [locally ringed space](c:locally-ringed-space), and so is every space that is locally isomorphic to a model.
An analytic space adds the condition that the local models are zero loci of analytic functions.
links.why: It shows that an analytic space is a locally ringed space with a specific local model.

reminder: André-Quillen homology is the homology of the cotangent complex of a ring map, with coefficients in a module.
definition: Let $A\to B$ be a homomorphism of commutative rings and let $M$ be a $B$-module. The André-Quillen homology is $D_n(B/A;M)=H_n(L_{B/A}\otimes_BM)$, where $L_{B/A}$ is the [cotangent complex](c:cotangent-complex), the [derived functor](c:derived-functor) version of the [Kähler differentials](c:kahler-differential) $\Omega_{B/A}$. In degree $0$, it is $D_0(B/A;M)=\Omega_{B/A}\otimes_BM$.
examples: The group $D_0(B/A;M)$ is the module of Kähler differentials with coefficients in $M$.
If $B$ is a polynomial ring over $A$, or a smooth $A$-algebra, then $D_n(B/A;M)=0$ for all $n>0$.
For $B=A/(f)$ with $f$ a nonzerodivisor, $D_1(B/A;B)=(f)/(f^2)$ and $D_n(B/A;B)=0$ for $n\ge2$.
Non-example: the module $\Omega_{B/A}$ alone is only $D_0$, so it is not André-Quillen homology, because it misses $D_1$ for $B=A/(f)$.

steps: Take a ring map $A\to B$ and a $B$-module $M$.
The cotangent complex $L_{B/A}$ has $H_0(L_{B/A})=\Omega_{B/A}$.
So $D_0(B/A;M)=\Omega_{B/A}\otimes_BM$, the [Kähler differentials](c:kahler-differential) with coefficients.
The higher groups $D_n$ with $n>0$ add information that vanishes when $B$ is smooth over $A$.
links.why: It shows that André-Quillen homology extends Kähler differentials to all degrees.

reminder: An antisymmetric wave function changes sign when two of its particle arguments are exchanged.
definition: A wave function $\psi(x_1,\dots,x_N)$ of $N$ identical particles is antisymmetric when exchanging any two arguments, a [transposition](c:transposition) of the arguments, changes its sign, that is, $\psi(\dots,x_i,\dots,x_j,\dots)=-\psi(\dots,x_j,\dots,x_i,\dots)$ for all $i\neq j$. Equivalently, $\psi\circ\sigma=\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\,\psi$ for every [permutation](c:permutation) $\sigma$ of the arguments, and $\psi$ vanishes when $x_i=x_j$, which is the Pauli exclusion principle for fermions.
examples: For two fermions in the orbitals $\phi_1$ and $\phi_2$, the function $\psi(x_1,x_2)=\phi_1(x_1)\phi_2(x_2)-\phi_2(x_1)\phi_1(x_2)$ is antisymmetric.
A Slater determinant $\det(\phi_j(x_i))$ is antisymmetric, because exchanging two rows of a [determinant](c:determinant) changes its sign.
The spin singlet $(\uparrow\downarrow-\downarrow\uparrow)/\sqrt2$ is antisymmetric under the exchange of the two spins.
Non-example: the function $\psi(x_1,x_2)=\phi(x_1)\phi(x_2)$ is symmetric, because exchange leaves it unchanged, and it is nonzero at $x_1=x_2$; it describes bosons.
